name: Law of the instrument
statement: Skill with a particular tool shapes which problems a person takes on, so the tool gets applied where it does not fit.
meaning: Abraham Kaplan's claim is about choosing problems rather than solving them. A researcher who is good at a technique will frame questions that technique can answer, and will treat the rest as somebody else's business. Kaplan set the point beside a line he quotes from R. A. Fisher, that a brilliant achievement 'may give a prestige to the method employed, or to some part of it, even in applications to which it has no special appropriateness'. His illustration is pilot selection: one psychologist runs depth interviews, a second uses projective tests, a third applies statistics to questionnaire data, a fourth dismisses the problem as practical rather than scientific, and a fifth works on a mathematical model of learning. He extends the argument to measurement on page 173, where 'the contemporary mystique of quantity' follows from owning subtle and powerful measuring techniques rather than from the subject matter requiring them. He names the mechanism on page 29: 'The price of training is always a certain "trained incapacity": the more we know how to do something, the harder it is to learn to do it differently.' Maslow's later version moves the emphasis from the person's training to the tool in hand, and it is the version that travelled.

origin.where: The Conduct of Inquiry: Methodology for Behavioral Science
origin.note: Kaplan names and states the law on page 28: 'I call it the law of the instrument, and it may be formulated as follows: Give a small boy a hammer, and he will find that everything he encounters needs pounding.' The book is not the first printing of the idea. Quote Investigator's earliest strong match is a June 1962 report in the Journal of Medical Education on an American Educational Research Association meeting held that February, giving Kaplan's spoken version as 'Give a boy a hammer and everything he meets has to be pounded'. Kenneth Mark Colby printed 'The First Law of the Instrument' in 1963, and Silvan Tomkins wrote 'If one has a hammer one tends to look for nails' in the same 1963 volume, three years before Maslow. None of those three documents was opened for this entry, and the 1962 report does not resolve at Crossref.

evidence: Nothing in the literature tests the law as Kaplan stated it. The nearest measured thing is the Einstellung effect, the mental set Abraham Luchins reported in 1942. Luchins gave water-jar problems solvable either by a long method learned on earlier items or by a short direct one. Across his six college groups, 70% to 100% of those who had worked through the long-method series used it again on the critical problems, against 0% in the two classes that served as controls, which used the direct method every time. Merim Bilalic, Peter McLeod and Fernand Gobet carried the paradigm into chess. Shown a position holding a familiar five-move smothered mate and an unfamiliar three-move mate, all six Grandmasters found the three-move mate, against 50% of six International Masters, 18% of 11 Masters and none of 11 Candidate Masters. A drop of 100 Elo points cut the odds of finding it by a factor of 3.67, B = .013, SE = .005, Z = 8.4, p = .004. Every one of those players found the three-move mate once the smothered mate was disabled by moving one bishop. Twelve other experts, mean Elo 2231, predicted that 86% of International Masters, 74% of Masters and 59% of Candidate Masters would find it, against actual figures of 50%, 18% and 0%. The familiar solution cost the experts about three standard deviations of playing strength. A companion study tracked the eyes of ten Candidate Masters, five per group. Players who had spotted the smothered mate all reported hunting for something shorter, and their gaze stayed on the squares belonging to the solution they already had, F(5, 20) = 0.6, not significant. Players given the version without the smothered mate shifted their gaze towards the squares that mattered, F(5, 20) = 11.9, p < .001, partial eta-squared .75. Heather Sheridan and Eyal Reingold ran the eye-tracking design again on 17 experts and 17 novices and found where it stops. Where the familiar move was merely suboptimal, 8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose it, and neither group looked away from it as the trial ran on. Where the familiar move was a blunder, every expert and most novices avoided it, and both groups disengaged over time.

replication.headline: No test of the law of the instrument was found, because nobody has turned it into a hypothesis; the nearest measured thing is the Einstellung effect, which is narrower than the law.
replication.detail: Searched on 17 August 2026. PubMed returns nothing for 'law of the instrument' in title or abstract, and 16 records for 'Maslow's hammer', all of them editorials, letters, comments, case reports or a study guide. Europe PMC's nearest relevant hit is a 2025 Radiology editorial. A Crossref bibliographic search under law of the instrument, Maslow's hammer and golden hammer returned legal scholarship, clinical commentary and management essays. Unpaywall was used only to check open copies of named papers. OpenAlex could not be searched because the account had no request budget left.

limits: The law is an aphorism about how researchers pick problems, and it has never been operationalised. The neighbouring work measures something smaller. Einstellung concerns one practised method inside one task, with the alternative sitting in the same problem. Functional fixedness, treated at no. 164, concerns one object and one unusual use of it. Neither asks whether owning a method changes which problems a person chooses to work on, which is what Kaplan asserted. The chess work also has a ceiling and a floor. Grandmasters, more than five standard deviations above average skill, all found the better move, and Sheridan and Reingold's effect vanished once the familiar move was a blunder rather than a merely inferior move. Bilalic and colleagues' own second experiment reports a residual cost that did not clear significance: players who had already met the two-solution problem took 148 s against 79 s to solve the one-solution version, t(8) = 1.67, p = .13, d = 1.2, and the effect reached significance only in a larger sample, t(44) = 2.16, p = .036, d = .65. Four documents wanted here were not obtained. Kaplan's 1964 Library Quarterly article returns 403 at the University of Chicago Press and Unpaywall lists no open copy, so its wording is quoted only at one remove. The 1963 Science review carrying Colby's sentence returns 403 at science.org. The June 1962 Journal of Medical Education report was not opened and does not resolve at Crossref. The 1868 Once a Week page was not read: Quote Investigator gives a page-level citation to a Google Books full-view scan for 18 April 1868, page 344, and neither the Google Books API nor the Internet Archive would return that volume during this task. So the oldest wording quoted on this page is Kaplan's.
misreadings: The sentence everyone quotes belongs to nobody. Maslow wrote 'I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail', which circulates as the tidier 'if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail'. Maslow never called it the law of the instrument, and the only Kaplan in the edition read here is Ann Kaplan on the copyright line. Nor was Maslow first to the word 'nail': Tomkins printed a version carrying it in 1963. Ralph Keyes, quoted by Quote Investigator, records the saying being credited 'to everyone from Buddha to Bernard Baruch', with Mark Twain the commonest recipient on no evidence. Kaplan also did not present the law as a straight failure. He wrote that it is 'by no means wholly pernicious in its working', asking with Peirce what else a person is to do with an idea but ride it hard and leave others to hold it back. Treating the law as identical to functional fixedness is the last error. Fixedness is failing to see a second use for an object on the table, and it is measured separately at no. 164. Kaplan's claim is that a researcher never puts the awkward problem on the table at all. The occupational version of the same claim sits at no. 181.

sources.text: Kaplan, A. (1964). The Conduct of Inquiry: Methodology for Behavioral Science. San Francisco: Chandler. The law is named and stated on page 28, qualified on page 29, and applied to measurement on pages 173 and 190. Read here from the Internet Archive's scan of the 1980 Sachin Publications reprint issued at Jaipur by arrangement with Thomas Y. Crowell, whose page 28 matches the page Quote Investigator verified in the Chandler edition.

Kaplan, A. (1964). The Age of the Symbol: A Philosophy of Library Education. The Library Quarterly, 34(4), 295-304. Quote Investigator quotes page 303 for a second 1964 formulation, 'give a small boy a hammer and it will turn out that everything he encounters needs pounding'. The article returns 403 at the University of Chicago Press and was not read for this entry.

Maslow, A. H. (1966). The Psychology of Science: A Reconnaissance. The hammer sentence sits in chapter 2, under the heading 'Problem-centering and method-centering: insistence on higher questions', after a comparison with a machine that washed cars and treated everything else that got into its clutches as a car. Read here from the Maurice Bassett digital edition, where it sits on page 14; Quote Investigator gives pages 15 and 16 in the Harper & Row printing.

Luchins, A. S. (1942). Mechanization in problem solving: The effect of Einstellung. Psychological Monographs, 54(6, Whole No. 248), i-95. Source of the water-jar figures above, read from the Internet Archive's scan of the issue. Unpaywall lists no open copy, and the scan is optical character recognition of a 1942 printing, so only figures legible on two separate downloads are quoted.

Bilalic, M., McLeod, P., & Gobet, F. (2008). Inflexibility of experts: Reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters. Cognitive Psychology, 56(2), 73-102. Source of the chess percentages, the logistic regression and the three standard deviations. Read from the authors' accepted manuscript in Brunel University's BURA repository, item 2438/641.

Bilalic, M., McLeod, P., & Gobet, F. (2008). Why good thoughts block better ones: The mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect. Cognition, 108(3), 652-661. Source of the eye-movement result and of the two solution-time comparisons. Read from the authors' accepted manuscript in Brunel University's BURA repository, item 2438/2276.

Sheridan, H., & Reingold, E. M. (2013). The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements. PLOS ONE, 8(10), e75796. Source of the expert and novice figures and of the blunder condition. Every number above was read from the article's JATS XML.

Duncker, K. (1945). On problem-solving. Psychological Monographs, 58(5), i-113. The source of functional fixedness; named here, not read, and measured at no. 164, which carries Duncker's and Adamson's solution rates.

Borko, H. (1963). Psychology's New Frontier: Computer Simulation of Personality. Silvan S. Tomkins and Samuel Messick, Ed. Wiley, New York, 1963. Science, 142(3593), 656. The review reprints Kenneth Mark Colby's 1963 statement of 'The First Law of the Instrument'. Returns 403 at science.org; the wording above is Quote Investigator's, at one remove.

Quote Investigator (2014, updated 2025). Quote Origin: If Your Only Tool Is a Hammer Then Every Problem Looks Like a Nail. Used here as an index to the 1868, 1962 and 1963 antecedents and for the Ralph Keyes line on misattribution, all at one remove.
